title: Low Back Pain - Red-Flag Screening and Differential Diagnosis
patient_instructions: You are David Harris, a 45-year-old warehouse worker with 5 days of lower back pain that started after lifting a heavy box at work. The pain is across the lower back, aching, worse with movement and bending, eased by rest and lying flat, and settles a little with paracetamol. It does NOT shoot down your legs today, and you have no numbness, tingling or weakness in your legs. Crucially (only reveal if asked directly): you have NO trouble passing or holding urine, no bowel incontinence, and NO numbness around the back passage or genitals. You have no fevers, no night sweats, no unexplained weight loss, no history of cancer, and you have not been unwell. No history of steroid use or IV drug use. Sleep is a little disturbed by pain but not worse at night specifically. Your ideas: you think you 'put your back out'. Your concerns: you are worried you have done serious damage to your spine and will not be able to work. Your expectation: you want a scan and strong painkillers. You are frustrated. If the candidate asks the 'red flag' questions, answer that all of those are absent. If the candidate asks about work and mood, admit you are stressed about missing work and money.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. David Harris, 45, presents with 5 days of mechanical-sounding low back pain after lifting at work. In 8 minutes: take a focused history that screens the important red flags for serious spinal pathology, form a working diagnosis, and briefly outline your initial management and safety-netting to the patient. You do not need to examine, but state what examination you would perform.
examiner_instructions: This tests red-flag screening for low back pain and evidence-based first-line management. Reward systematic screening for cauda equina syndrome (bladder/bowel dysfunction, saddle anaesthesia, bilateral/progressive leg weakness), malignancy (age, prior cancer, weight loss, night pain), infection (fever, IV drug use, immunosuppression) and inflammatory back pain (age <40, insidious onset, morning stiffness >30 min, improves with exercise). The presenting scenario is non-specific mechanical back pain. Reward the candidate stating that cauda equina is a time-critical surgical emergency needing same-day MRI and emergency spinal referral, and that they would do a PR exam for anal tone/perianal sensation. Reward correct first-line management: advise staying active and avoid bed rest, short course of oral NSAID (e.g. ibuprofen 400 mg up to TDS) with PPI cover if GI risk - NOT paracetamol monotherapy - and screening yellow flags. Reassure it is not sinister rather than saying it is 'not related to the spine'. Prompt: 'Which single feature would make you send him to hospital today?'

criteria: Characterises the pain (SOCRATES) and mechanism and screens for radicular/neurological symptoms
Systematically screens cauda equina red flags (bladder/bowel, saddle anaesthesia, bilateral/progressive weakness)
Screens malignancy, infection and inflammatory back pain features and assesses psychosocial yellow flags
Reaches a working diagnosis of non-specific (mechanical) low back pain given absent red flags
Correctly explains mechanical pain arises from spinal structures and is not sinister (not 'unrelated to the spine')
Identifies which findings would change the diagnosis (radiculopathy, malignancy, AS, cauda equina)
First-line: stay active, avoid bed rest, short course oral NSAID (not paracetamol monotherapy) with PPI cover if GI risk; structured physiotherapy/exercise
Recognises cauda equina as a same-day surgical emergency (urgent MRI, emergency spinal referral, PR exam) and advises ED/000 if acute urinary retention
Appropriate imaging stance (no routine early imaging without red flags) and clear safety-netting
Reassures accurately and manages expectations about scans/opioids
Addresses return-to-work concerns and checks understanding

red_flags: Cauda equina syndrome - urinary retention/incontinence, faecal incontinence, saddle (perineal) anaesthesia, bilateral or progressive leg weakness: same-day MRI and emergency spinal referral
Malignancy - age >50 with new pain, past cancer, unexplained weight loss, night pain, thoracic point tenderness (consider metastatic cord compression)
Infection - fever, IV drug use, immunosuppression, recent bacteraemia (discitis/epidural abscess)
Inflammatory back pain - age <40, insidious onset, morning stiffness >30 min, improvement with exercise (axial spondyloarthritis)
australian_guidelines: eTG / 2018 Lancet low back pain series: paracetamol monotherapy is not effective for acute low back pain; first-line pharmacological therapy is a short course of an oral NSAID at the lowest effective dose with PPI cover if GI risk

RACGP: advise staying active and avoiding bed rest; do not routinely image non-specific low back pain without red flags; use structured physiotherapy/exercise rather than routine chiropractic manipulation

Cauda equina syndrome is a time-critical surgical emergency - urgent (same-day) MRI, PR examination for anal tone/perianal sensation, emergency neurosurgical/spinal referral; decompression within 24-48 h preserves function
Screen psychosocial yellow flags (STarT Back) as predictors of chronicity; for suspected axial spondyloarthritis check CRP/ESR, HLA-B27 and SI-joint imaging with rheumatology referral
learning_objectives: Perform structured red-flag screening for low back pain across cauda equina, malignancy, infection and inflammatory causes
Apply current evidence-based first-line management (stay active + NSAID, not paracetamol monotherapy)
Recognise cauda equina syndrome as a same-day surgical emergency
Reassure accurately and address psychosocial yellow flags and return-to-work
key_points: Paracetamol monotherapy is no longer recommended for acute low back pain; use a short NSAID course with PPI cover if GI risk
Cauda equina syndrome needs same-day MRI and emergency spinal referral; do a PR exam and advise ED/000 if acute retention
Do not routinely image non-specific low back pain without red flags
Mechanical back pain arises from spinal structures - reassure it is not sinister, not that it is 'unrelated to the spine'
Screen yellow flags; advise staying active and structured physiotherapy over routine manipulation

citations.claim: Low back pain should be worked up with a structured diagnostic strategy in which non-specific vertebral dysfunction is the probability diagnosis while serious causes (malignancy, infection, fracture) are actively excluded.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.789

citations.claim: Cauda equina features - bladder/bowel disturbance, perineal (saddle) sensory change and progressive motor deficit - are absolute indications for urgent surgical intervention in radiculopathy.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.830

citations.claim: A large central disc protrusion can cause bladder symptoms/incontinence and S1 root lesions warrant suspicion for malignancy, linking radicular signs, cauda equina and metastatic red flags.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.832
